articles.headline: El Concello de Lugo actúa de urgencia ante las casas ruinosas repartidas por la ciudad
articles.subtitle: Urbanismo interviene en la calle Rúa do Carme tras detectar una grieta peligrosa en una vivienda vallada y mantiene la vigilancia sobre el muro del colegio Quiroga Ballesteros y la tapia de Frigsa, con catas y estudios geotécnicos en marcha.
articles.body:
El Concello de Lugo ha pasado a la acción ante las casas ruinosas que salpican la ciudad. El área de Urbanismo intervino esta semana en la calle Rúa do Carme, donde una vivienda vallada presentaba una grieta peligrosa en la medianera: los operarios retiraron la galería y parte del muro en riesgo de caída, una actuación que los concejales Ramón Cabarcos y María Reigosa supervisaron sobre el terreno.

No es el único punto bajo vigilancia. El muro del colegio Quiroga Ballesteros lleva más de dos años apuntalado y sigue pendiente de una solución definitiva, mientras la tapia de la antigua fábrica de Frigsa permanece vallada desde hace meses a la espera de las catas y del estudio geotécnico encargado por el área de Infraestruturas, que confirmó que el daño es mayor de lo previsto.

A ellas se suman una casa apuntalada en la Praza do Campo, en plena rehabilitación, y los daños del incendio declarado este verano en el restaurante Antas. El gobierno local recuerda que aprobó el año pasado una ordenanza para obligar a los propietarios a mantener sus inmuebles y que prepara un plan especial para los barrios de A Milagrosa y Feijoo.

articles.headline: La ocupación hotelera de Lugo roza el 87% este verano, aunque la patronal percibe contención del gasto
articles.subtitle: Los hoteles de la provincia promedian el 87% de ocupación entre julio y agosto, con picos del cien por cien, pero las estancias se acortan y los clientes moderan el gasto; septiembre arranca con la primera quincena ya reservada.
articles.body:
Los hoteles de la provincia de Lugo rozan el 87% de ocupación media entre julio y agosto, con picos que superan el 90% y que llegaron al cien por cien entre el 15 de julio y el 15 de agosto, según los datos que maneja la Asociación Provincial de Empresarios da Hostalería. El presidente del colectivo, Cheché Real, destaca que la demanda se mantuvo en A Mariña, la Ribeira Sacra y la capital.

El eclipse del 12 de agosto dejó una ocupación casi plena y trajo a la provincia visitantes de toda Europa, incluidos turistas de Estados Unidos y Canadá, algo que la patronal considera una novedad. Aun así, el sector percibe contención del gasto: las estancias se acortan, de un mes a dos o tres semanas, y los clientes modulan lo que gastan en restaurantes y servicios.

Los datos oficiales respaldan la tendencia: el INE contabilizó en julio 1.334.577 pernoctaciones en Galicia, un 0,68% más que el año pasado, de las que 96.636 corresponden a Lugo, y los ingresos por habitación ocupada marcaron un récord de 91,30 euros. Septiembre apunta bien: la primera quincena ya figura como temporada alta.

articles.headline: Más de 700 concentraciones en toda España reivindican este miércoles la defensa de Ceuta
articles.subtitle: El PP convoca movilizaciones con motivo del Día de Ceuta y reúne de nuevo en la calle a Feijóo y Abascal; alcaldes socialistas se suman pese a Ferraz y el acto de Cibeles se reconvierte en institucional tras el veto de la Delegación del Gobierno.
articles.body:
España se vuelca este miércoles con Ceuta. Más de 700 concentraciones convocadas por el PP, con el apoyo de Vox y otras formaciones, se celebran a lo largo del día en toda España con motivo del Día de Ceuta, en una jornada en la que la oposición reclama al Gobierno medidas concretas ante la crisis migratoria y el colapso de los servicios de la ciudad.

La cita central en Madrid reúne de nuevo en la calle a Alberto Núñez Feijóo y Santiago Abascal, tres años después de las concentraciones contra la amnistía, según destaca El Mundo. El acto de la Puerta de Alcalá se reconvirtió en un evento institucional: la Delegación del Gobierno no autorizó la manifestación al considerar que el Ayuntamiento de Madrid, convocante, no es titular del derecho de reunión, como recoge Europa Press.

La jornada cuenta además con la adhesión de varios alcaldes socialistas que han decidido sumarse pese al criterio de Ferraz, en un gesto que subraya la división interna del PSOE. El PP aprovecha la fecha para exigir la reprobación del Gobierno y un plan de choque para Ceuta, mientras la oposición mantiene la presión sobre el Ejecutivo.

articles.headline: La Policía informa al juez de que Marruecos planificó el salto de Ceuta y Marlaska pide explicaciones
articles.subtitle: Un informe del CENIF remitido a la jueza de instrucción número 7 de Ceuta sostiene que gendarmes marroquíes guiaron y coordinaron la avalancha para colapsar el sistema fronterizo; el ministro del Interior reclama cuentas a la Policía tras conocerse el documento.
articles.body:
La entrada masiva de migrantes en Ceuta del pasado 30 de julio fue planificada y ejecutada por agentes marroquíes, según un informe del CENIF, el centro de inteligencia contra el terrorismo y el crimen organizado, remitido a la jueza María Tardón, titular del juzgado de instrucción número 7 de la ciudad. El documento, al que ha tenido acceso El Mundo, sostiene que gendarmes de Marruecos guiaron y coordinaron el salto para colapsar el sistema de control fronterizo.

El contenido del informe ha encendido al ministro del Interior. Fernando Grande-Marlaska pidió explicaciones por escrito a la Policía tras conocerse que la entrada habría sido organizada desde el otro lado de la valla, en un movimiento que eleva la tensión entre Interior y los cuerpos policiales, según recoge 20minutos.

El Ejecutivo evita por ahora pronunciarse sobre la autoría y mantiene el discurso de la desestabilización, mientras la oposición reclama que el Congreso conozca el informe íntegro. La crisis, que dejó a miles de migrantes en la calle durante semanas, sigue condicionando la agenda política y la relación con Marruecos.

articles.headline: Bruselas no ve pruebas de que la crisis de Ceuta fuera provocada por desinformación extranjera
articles.subtitle: El Servicio Europeo de Acción Exterior constata intentos de Rusia de sacar partido a la crisis en redes desde el 30 de julio, pero no encuentra evidencia concluyente de que la avalancha fuera orquestada desde el exterior, lo que matiza la tesis de Sánchez.
articles.body:
Bruselas matiza la versión del Gobierno sobre la crisis de Ceuta. El Servicio Europeo de Acción Exterior (SEAE) asegura que no existe una evidencia concluyente de que la entrada masiva de migrantes fuera provocada por desinformación de actores estatales extranjeros, aunque sí constata intentos posteriores de Rusia de sacar partido de la situación en las redes sociales, según informa Europa Press.

El SEAE detectó desde el 30 de julio campañas con bots y cuentas falsas que difundían contenido prorruso y mensajes destinados a avivar las divisiones sobre migración, pero no pruebas de que esos actores orquestaran la avalancha. La UE no quiso comentar las acusaciones contra Israel, otro de los países señalados por el presidente del Gobierno.

Las declaraciones contrastan con la tesis que Pedro Sánchez defendió el lunes, cuando atribuyó la crisis a una operación de desestabilización rusa basándose en informes del SEAE. El País y El Mundo subrayan el matiz: la UE confirma la explotación posterior, pero no la autoría inicial, en un episodio que reabre el debate sobre la gestión de la crisis.

articles.headline: El alga tropical Asparagopsis taxiformis llega por primera vez a las costas de Galicia
articles.subtitle: Investigadores del IEO-CSIC confirman el primer hallazgo en Galicia de esta macroalga invasora del Indopacífico, localizada en O Grove; amplía 500 kilómetros su rango conocido en el Atlántico y se teme su expansión con la tropicalización del litoral.
articles.body:
Una nueva especie invasora ha llegado a las costas gallegas. Científicos del Centro Oceanográfico de Vigo, del IEO-CSIC, confirmaron la presencia en O Grove de la macroalga tropical Asparagopsis taxiformis, una especie originaria del Indopacífico que ahora amplía unos 500 kilómetros su rango conocido en el Atlántico, según publica la revista Bioinvasions Records.

La investigadora Eva Cacabelos, autora principal del estudio, explica que el ejemplar hallado pertenece al linaje 2, el de mayor tolerancia ambiental y capacidad invasora. La población localizada es todavía incipiente, sin estructuras reproductoras, lo que da margen para actuar, pero los expertos advierten del riesgo de coinvasión con otras especies como Rugulopteryx okamurae.

El hallazgo, recogido también por el IEO-CSIC y Faro de Vigo, se enmarca en la tropicalización del litoral impulsada por el cambio climático, que acerca cada vez más especies de aguas cálidas a la costa gallega. Los científicos piden colaboración ciudadana a través de la plataforma Observadores del Mar y recomiendan no arrancar los ejemplares para evitar su dispersión.

articles.headline: Bryant orders independent review of the Parades Commission after Drumcree ruling
articles.subtitle: The Secretary of State announces a judge-led review of the Parades Commission after the High Court quashed its Drumcree determination; the body keeps the Government's full backing while six commissioner posts are opened to public appointment.
articles.body:
Sir Chris Bryant has ordered an independent, judge-led review of the Parades Commission, weeks after the High Court quashed its determination on the Drumcree parade at Garvaghy Road. The Secretary of State announced the review as he confirmed that the commission retains the Government's full backing for the remainder of this year's parade season, according to the BBC.

The review will examine how the commission reaches its determinations and how it can restore public confidence, with the findings expected to shape the body's future. In the meantime, six commissioner posts whose terms are ending will be opened to public appointment, a process the Irish News reports has already drawn criticism from unionists who wanted the commission overhauled rather than refreshed.

The DUP's Gavin Robinson said commissioners had lost all credibility and should stand aside, while the Orange Order had earlier called for resignations after the court ruling. Bryant said the review was not about finding fault but about ensuring parading is managed in a way that commands respect from all communities in Northern Ireland.

articles.headline: Teachers' unions vote for strike action over workload as schools return
articles.subtitle: Five unions backed industrial action in ballots over the Department of Education's failure to implement the 27 recommendations of the independent workload review; no strike dates are set yet, and the minister is urged to act before schools feel the impact.
articles.body:
Teachers across Northern Ireland have voted overwhelmingly for strike action over workload, in ballots timed as pupils return to classrooms. The NASUWT reported 92.04% of members backing strikes and 98.63% supporting action short of strike, on a 54.89% turnout, while the INTO recorded 91% and 99% respectively and the UTU 71% and 95%, with the NAHT also backing action, the BBC reports.

The unions argue that the Department of Education has failed to implement the 27 recommendations of the independent review of teacher workload published last November, which they say would reduce excessive hours and improve retention. The Irish News reports that action short of strike is expected to begin with teachers declining tasks such as cover supervision and after-hours meetings.

No strike dates have been set, and the unions say they remain open to talks with Education Minister Paul Givan, who has been urged to act before the industrial action escalates. The INTO's Mark McTaggart said members had sent an unmissable message, while the NEU is expected to announce the results of its own ballot shortly, according to RTÉ.

articles.headline: Derry and Strabane face the North's most acute peace challenge, landmark index finds
articles.subtitle: The first Northern Ireland Peace Index shows violence fell 10.7% since 2019, but researchers find the north-west district records the highest paramilitary activity and homicide rates, even as its hate crime figures improve sharply.
articles.body:
The first Northern Ireland Peace Index, published by the Institute for Economics and Peace with Queen's University Belfast, finds that negative peace, the absence of violence, improved by 10.7% between 2019 and now, taking the composite score from 2.14 to 1.91, the lowest since the index began. Hate crime was the only indicator to worsen overall across the region.

The report highlights Derry City and Strabane as presenting the most acute combined peace challenge in the North. The district records the highest rate of paramilitary activity, around three times the regional average and above Belfast, and a homicide rate roughly two and a half times the Northern Ireland average, according to the Derry Journal. Its positive peace score, measuring social foundations, is also the weakest.

There is good news too: Derry and Strabane recorded the largest improvements in violence and saw hate crime fall by about 20%. Belfast, by contrast, has the strongest positive peace but the highest concentration of violence. The researchers, Dr Andrew Thomson and Professor Dominic Bryan, say the index gives councils a tool to target investment where peace is weakest, the Belfast Telegraph reports.

articles.headline: Iran hits US bases in Jordan and Bahrain as Washington bombs IRGC targets again
articles.subtitle: Tehran launches drones at Camp Titin in Jordan and Sheikh Isa in Bahrain after US strikes killed four people at a wedding party in Sirik; Washington carries out a second wave of strikes on Revolutionary Guard targets within 48 hours, fuelling fears of wider war.
articles.body:
The United States and Iran have traded a new round of strikes, deepening fears of a wider conflict in the Gulf. Washington bombed Revolutionary Guard targets in Iran for the second time in 48 hours, an operation in which four people were killed at a wedding party in the coastal town of Sirik, on the Strait of Hormuz, according to the BBC.

Tehran responded by launching drones at US bases in the region: Camp Titin in Jordan, near Aqaba, was hit for the second time in days, and Sheikh Isa airbase in Bahrain was struck for the first time, as El Mundo reports. The Pentagon confirmed the attacks and said US forces were assessing the damage, while the White House warned that further strikes would follow if attacks continued.

The exchange comes after the collapse of the memorandum that had governed Iran's cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog, and as oil markets watch the Strait of Hormuz nervously. Both sides say they do not want an all-out war, but The Guardian notes the escalation has put the region on a hair trigger, with Washington also weighing new sanctions against Tehran's economy.

articles.headline: Germany blames Russia for the Leipzig airport drone attack and closes its Bonn consulate
articles.subtitle: Berlin concludes that Russian agents were behind the drone strike that shut Leipzig/Halle airport, closing Russia's consulate in Bonn and ending the Russian House contract; Moscow denies involvement as NATO and the EU rally behind Germany.
articles.body:
Germany has formally blamed Russian agents for the drone attack that shut down Leipzig/Halle airport last September, halting flights for around eight hours and injuring a drone pilot. The government in Berlin said the evidence pointed to a state-organised operation and announced a package of retaliatory measures, the BBC reports.

The measures include closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, terminating the contract for the Russian House cultural centre in Leipzig and tightening entry rules for Russian citizens. Moscow denied any involvement, with the Kremlin describing the accusations as baseless, while NATO and the EU expressed full solidarity with Germany, as Europa Press and The Guardian report.

The attribution is the first time Berlin has publicly pinned a hybrid attack on Russia since the war in Ukraine began, and it is expected to feed into the EU's debate on countering hybrid threats. German officials said further diplomatic steps were possible if Russia continued its campaign of sabotage and espionage on European soil.

articles.headline: Haakon VIII is proclaimed King of Norway after taking the oath before the Storting
articles.subtitle: The 53-year-old monarch swears to govern Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, days after the death of his father Harald V at 89; the ceremony in Oslo was attended by the government, parliament and the royal family, with the crown princess watching on.
articles.body:
Haakon VIII was proclaimed King of Norway on Tuesday after taking the constitutional oath before the Storting in Oslo. Flanked by the government and the royal family, the 53-year-old monarch swore that he would govern the Kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and its laws, bringing to a close the brief interregnum that followed the death of his father, as the AP reports.

Harald V, who reigned for 35 years and was Europe's oldest living monarch at 89, died last Friday, prompting a period of national mourning. Speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the proclamation to parliament, and the ceremony was attended by Queen Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, who watched her father take the oath that her great-grandfather, grandfather and father each took before her.

The new king's accession is the first since 1991, when Harald himself took the oath after the death of Olav V. The BBC reports that thousands of Norwegians lined the streets of Oslo to pay their respects, with the royal palace receiving a steady stream of mourners throughout the day.

articles.headline: US Congress moves to avert a government shutdown weeks before the midterms
articles.subtitle: The House passes a stopgap funding bill that keeps the government open into December, clearing the way for the Senate; the vote heads off a shutdown that would have hit federal services just before the November elections.
articles.body:
The House of Representatives passed a stopgap funding bill on Tuesday that would keep the US government open into December, in a bipartisan vote that clears the way for the Senate to act before the deadline. The continuing resolution funds agencies at current levels and avoids the shutdown that would otherwise have begun at the end of the month, The Guardian reports.

The timing is politically loaded: a shutdown just weeks before the November midterm elections would have closed federal services, delayed pay for hundreds of thousands of workers and given both parties an unpredictable campaign issue. The bill passed with support from both sides of the aisle, a sign of how eager lawmakers were to avoid that scenario.

The measure now heads to the Senate, where leaders in both parties have signalled they will back it. It is the latest in a series of short-term extensions that have kept Washington funded through the year, and El Correo Gallego notes the deal hands both parties a modest win as they head into the campaign stretch.

articles.headline: John Ternus teases a 'huge launch' next week in his first memo as Apple CEO
articles.subtitle: Apple's new chief executive, who succeeds Tim Cook after fifteen years, tells staff a huge launch is coming next week; the September 9 event is expected to bring the company's first foldable iPhone and a Gemini-powered Siri overhaul.
articles.body:
Apple's new chief executive, John Ternus, has marked his first days in the job with a memo to employees teasing a huge launch next week, according to TechCrunch. The message lands days before Apple's September 9 event, which is widely expected to introduce the company's first foldable iPhone along with a major Siri overhaul powered by Google's Gemini models.

Ternus, who previously ran hardware engineering, succeeds Tim Cook, who steps down after fifteen years as CEO to become executive chairman. The transition comes amid a wave of executive departures, including Phil Schiller, the long-serving head of the App Store, who is among those leaving as the company reshapes its leadership under its new chief.

In his memo, Ternus said Apple was in the strongest position in its history and urged employees to focus on the products ahead. Analysts read the note as an attempt to steady the company after months of uncertainty, with the foldable iPhone seen as the first big test of whether Apple can still define a category rather than follow one.

articles.headline: Waymo goes on the offensive days before Tesla's Cybercab launch
articles.subtitle: The Alphabet-owned robotaxi operator says cameras alone cannot deliver full autonomy and announces three new markets, as Tesla prepares to add its two-seater, steering-wheel-free Cybercab to its Austin fleet at a September 3 launch event.
articles.body:
Waymo has taken aim at Tesla just days before the launch of the Cybercab. In a blog post and an interview with Axios, the Alphabet-owned robotaxi operator argued that fully autonomous driving is not possible with cameras alone, calling pure end-to-end systems a black box risk. Cameras are incredible, but they aren't enough, wrote Srikanth Thirumalai, the vice president who oversees Waymo's driving software.

The company also announced three new markets on Tuesday, extending a network that already serves more than a dozen US cities with around 3,000 vehicles and over 500,000 paid trips a week. The contrast with Tesla is stark: Waymo says it has logged more than 220 million rider-only miles, while Tesla's unsupervised fleet has driven roughly 380,000, according to The Verge.

Tesla, for its part, is pressing ahead with the Cybercab, a two-seater with no steering wheel or pedals, rated at 165 watt-hours per mile. The company confirmed a September 3 launch event in Austin and has begun registering Cybercabs with the Texas DMV, though Electrek notes the fleet remains tiny and the event may be more spectacle than scale.

articles.headline: AfterQuery becomes Y Combinator's fastest-ever unicorn at a $3.2 billion valuation
articles.subtitle: The 18-month-old AI training-data startup founded by two twentysomethings has seen its valuation rise more than tenfold since April, in a round first reported by Forbes; expert human reasoning has become the AI industry's scarcest input.
articles.body:
AfterQuery has raised a round valuing the AI training-data startup at $3.2 billion, making it the fastest company in Y Combinator's history to go from launch to unicorn status, Forbes first reported. The valuation is more than ten times the $300 million the company was worth in April, when it announced a $30 million Series A led by Altos Ventures.

The startup was founded in February 2025 by Spencer Mateega and Carlos Georgescu, then still teenagers, who went through Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort. Rather than simple annotation, AfterQuery employs doctors, lawyers and other specialists to produce training data that encodes how professionals reason through hard problems, a niche that has become the industry's most sought-after input.

Customers include Nvidia, Legora and the Korean lab Motif Technologies, and the company said in April it had passed $100 million in annualised revenue. YC partner Gustaf Alströmer called the pace remarkable even by 2026 standards, and analysts see the round as fresh evidence that the bottleneck in AI is no longer compute but expert human work, TechCrunch notes.

articles.headline: X probes a wave of password-reset emails targeting accounts after X Money's rollout
articles.subtitle: Users report unsolicited reset emails and confirmation codes just as X Money expands to US subscribers; X says attackers appear to believe the payment service makes accounts more valuable, and urges users to enable password reset protection and two-factor authentication.
articles.body:
X is investigating a wave of unsolicited password-reset emails that hit users on Tuesday, shortly after the payment service X Money expanded to US Premium and Premium+ subscribers. Dozens of users reported receiving ten or more reset messages and confirmation codes within hours, prompting fears of a coordinated attempt to take over accounts, TechCrunch reports.

Mridul Singhai, a product engineer at X, said the company had found no evidence of a breach so far and that attackers appear to believe the wider availability of X Money makes accounts more valuable. He said the reset forms were being mass-triggered using public usernames, and X's general counsel, James Burnham, promised the legal team would stop at nothing to hold those responsible to account.

Security experts and outlets including PCMag advise users not to click links in the emails and to enable two-factor authentication and X's password reset protection feature, which requires confirmation before a reset link is sent. The incident is the latest reminder that where money flows, attackers follow, as X prepares to expand X Money beyond the United States.

articles.headline: OpenAI's Astra is its first model to hit 'critical' cyber capabilities — locked down at launch
articles.subtitle: OpenAI says Astra can find and exploit unknown security flaws without human guidance, the first model to meet its critical cybersecurity threshold; the advanced capabilities are limited to early-access partners at launch, with a general release to follow soon.
articles.body:
OpenAI has announced that Astra, its forthcoming frontier model, is the first to meet the critical cybersecurity threshold in the company's safety framework. In a blog post laying out the model's capabilities, OpenAI said Astra can identify and exploit unknown vulnerabilities without human guidance, scoring perfectly on the ExploitBench benchmark and finding two zero-day flaws in a modified test environment.

Because of the risk, the advanced cyber capabilities will not be part of the general release, which OpenAI says will come soon. Instead, they will be available at launch only to select partners in Daybreak Blue, an early-access programme for organisations working on defensive security, as Wired reports. The company describes Astra as its most aligned model to date, with chain-of-thought monitoring designed to catch misuse.

The announcement is a milestone in the debate over AI and security, coming after OpenAI's 2025 response to the Hugging Face breakout incident. The OpenAI Foundation's Yona Shavit said the capabilities would be useful to defenders facing increasingly sophisticated attacks, while researchers caution that the same technology could lower the barrier for offensive hacking.

articles.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.1 with 75% cheaper cache reads and a restricted Mythos 5.1
articles.subtitle: Fable 5.1 is generally available with cache-read prices cut 75%, making typical workloads about 25% cheaper, while the safety-first Mythos 5.1 sibling posts big gains on terminal and scientific benchmarks but stays restricted to select US organisations.
articles.body:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.1, the newest version of its flagship model, alongside a restricted sibling called Mythos 5.1. Fable 5.1 is generally available with a 75% cut to cache-read prices, which Anthropic says makes typical workloads around 25% cheaper and agentic workloads up to 45% cheaper, a significant reduction for heavy users.

Mythos 5.1, which shares the same base weights but carries stricter safeguards around cyber and life-science capabilities, is limited to US organisations and excludes automated access. On benchmarks, Mythos 5.1 reaches 60.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 52.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science, while Fable 5.1 posts strong gains on AutomationBench, and Anthropic reports a roughly 50% hit rate on protein-binder design tasks.

The release also introduces Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, letting organisations run the models in customer-controlled cloud environments, and follows a period in which Anthropic has been under pressure to show its models can justify their price tag. TechCrunch notes the cheaper cache reads are aimed squarely at developers running long, agentic workflows.

articles.headline: Thinking longer lets frontier models recall up to 65% of facts they already know, Google study finds
articles.subtitle: Knowledge profiling of 13 language models on the new WikiProfile benchmark shows GPT-5 and Gemini-3 encode 95–98% of facts yet fail to directly recall a quarter of them; giving models time to think recovers 40–65% of that forgotten knowledge.
articles.body:
A study by Google Research and the Technion suggests that when large language models get facts wrong, the knowledge is often not missing at all, it is simply hard to reach. Using a new benchmark called WikiProfile, built from 2,150 Wikipedia-derived facts, the researchers profiled 13 models across more than four million responses, distinguishing whether a fact is encoded in the weights or actually recallable.

The results show frontier models such as GPT-5 and Gemini-3 encode 95–98% of the tested facts, yet fail to directly recall between a quarter and a third of them without extra computation. The authors frame it as empty shelves versus lost keys: scaling model size fills the shelves, but recall failures persist and even grow, as the group found when scaling Gemma3 from one billion to 27 billion parameters.

The good news is that inference-time thinking recovers 40–65% of encoded-but-unrecalled facts, and the gains are biggest for rare facts and reverse questions. VentureBeat reports the researchers argue companies should route queries to deeper reasoning selectively rather than globally, since models still lack the self-awareness to know when they are about to fail.

articles.headline: ChatGPT for Healthcare plugs into Epic's records and nine public health data sources
articles.subtitle: OpenAI's read-only Epic integration gives clinicians access to patient records covering more than 325 million people, with ChatGPT available inside the electronic health record in some deployments; a new plugin adds ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, RxNorm and more.
articles.body:
OpenAI has connected ChatGPT for Healthcare to Epic, the electronic health record system used by hospitals covering more than 325 million patients. The read-only integration lets clinicians pull appointment notes, laboratory results, medications and specialist documentation into ChatGPT to summarise developments and prepare for visits, and in some deployments the assistant appears directly inside the EHR workflow.

The company also launched a Healthcare Public Data plugin that connects ChatGPT and Codex to nine official sources, including ClinicalTrials.gov, CMS Coverage, RxNorm, DailyMed and PubMed, allowing teams to verify precise details like trial eligibility or coverage policy versions without hunting across sites. Organisations with a business associate agreement can use the tools in HIPAA-compliant workspaces.

OpenAI said physicians rated 99.1% of responses safe across 4,363 evaluations covering 27 clinical use cases, with more than 93% rated good or better on accuracy across five connected data sources. Fierce Healthcare reports that pilot partners including UCLA Health are exploring how the integration can cut the time clinicians spend synthesising records.

articles.headline: The ChatGPT desktop app quietly bundles a full copy of LibreOffice
articles.subtitle: Simon Willison discovers a 1.7GB runtime in the Codex cache that ships Python, Node.js, Poppler, git and the LibreOffice suite, letting the agent read and render office documents; a GitHub issue reveals the bundled copy is broken on some Macs.
articles.body:
The ChatGPT desktop app, formerly the Codex app, quietly ships a full copy of LibreOffice. Simon Willison discovered the bundle while poking around his cache folder, finding a 1.7GB runtime containing a complete Python installation, Node.js, Poppler, git and native LibreOffice binaries, along with skills that tell the agent how to use them to read and render office documents.

The discovery explains how ChatGPT manages to open, convert and visually render Word and Excel files, and it sparked a lively discussion on Hacker News about licensing and engineering trade-offs: LibreOffice is distributed under the Mozilla Public License, so bundling it is legal, but shipping a whole office suite to render a docx file struck many as heavy.

There is a wrinkle, though: a GitHub issue reports that the bundled LibreOffice runtime is broken on macOS, because it links against Homebrew libraries that are not present on machines without Homebrew, breaking document rendering. For now, the workaround is to point the agent at a system installation of LibreOffice instead.
